description: We are an ambitious, multidisciplinary team of talented individuals, each bringing unique skills and strengths to the table. Our team combines expertise in language, coding, web development, game development, graphic design, LARPing, space, and physics. By bringing together diverse perspectives and creative approaches, we aim to tackle challenges in innovative and unconventional ways.
summary:
ProjectSpacer follows NASA's four mission segments. Players pick one of 13 missions on real problems (deforestation, wildfires, storms, radiation belts, asteroids), build a CubeSat from 50+ parts modelled on real CubeSat products with approximate real mass, power and price, plan the orbit with two-body mechanics, program the satellite with WHEN/DO blocks, fly a rideshare launch, hold attitude during the orbit burn and run mission control from Ulaanbaatar.

Our main innovation is the report engine. It reads every installed part, small choices (solar wing size, launch heading, release time) and the player's own algorithm, then runs 100 scenarios of weather, outages and anomalies minute by minute (~4.5 million simulated minutes, ~2-3 s in the browser). It picks from 34 finding types across 13 missions (over 200 billion combinations), tags each claim RECORDED, PROJECTED or ASSUMED, and re-tests the best fix (e.g. radio to dish: 0% to 91%). Validated against a full simulation: 7/7 designs agree.

Impact: students feel how one choice changes mass, power, data and cost. The game never says "wrong"; it explains why.

Tools: Unity 6 (C#, WebGL), Blender. Values are simplified for learning.

Code in this project was written with assistance from AI tools (Claude Code) and reviewed by the team.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ProjectSpacer is a browser game where players design a small science mission from start to finish, following the four segments (Launch, Space, Ground, User) and six steps in NASA's "Design and Develop Science Missions" guide.

1. Mission: choose one of 13 missions that address real problems: desertification, deforestation, wildfires, melting ice and storms (Easy, Earth observation); radiation belts, the South Atlantic Anomaly and particle alerts (Medium, space weather); lunar mapping, asteroid tracking and variable stars (Hard, space telescopes). Each brief gives the need, goals, concept, measurable requirements and who uses the data.

2. Build: assemble a CubeSat in a 3D clean room from 50+ parts modelled on real commercial CubeSat products (e.g. HyperScout 2, MultiScape100, Sagitta, RWP015, TRXVU, iOBC) with approximate real-world mass, size, power, data rate and price. Mass, volume, budget and power update live; nothing is forbidden.

3. Orbit: set altitude and launch heading; two-body orbital mechanics gives inclination, period, lifetime and passes over each target.

4. Code: program the satellite with WHEN -> DO blocks and test it in a 24-hour simulation (images, downlinks, battery, storage, eclipse heating).

5-6. Launch and fly: rideshare launch, then hold the satellite steady during the orbit burn; difficulty depends on the installed reaction wheels and mass.

7. Ground: point the Ulaanbaatar dish, check every subsystem, upload the program and receive first light.

8. Report: the core of the project (see below).

THE REPORT ENGINE (our main innovation)

Every mission ends with a report written for that exact design. It takes every installed part and its specs, small choices (solar cell type and wing size, launch heading, release time) and the player's own algorithm, then runs 100 scenarios with varied weather, station outages, anomalies and solar output, minute by minute (about 4.5 million simulated minutes per report, computed in ~2-3 s in the browser). It selects from 34 types of findings across 13 missions (over 200 billion possible combinations), ranks them by severity, tags every claim RECORDED, PROJECTED or ASSUMED, and re-tests the best fix on the same seeds (e.g. "Replace the radio with the High-Gain Dish Antenna: 0% -> 91%"). Fix & Retry restores the build in one click. The fast model was validated against a full minute-by-minute simulation: 7 of 7 test designs agree, largest gap 0.08 (limit 0.10).

WHY IT MATTERS

The challenge asks players to feel how one decision affects everything else. A better camera adds mass, power and data, and is useless if the radio cannot send the data home. Players discover these trade-offs themselves; the game never says "wrong", it explains why. There is no single right mission, only trade-offs you can prove.

TOOLS

Unity 6 (C#, URP, WebGL), Blender (Python-scripted models), itch.io hosting. Orbit, coding and analysis logic are engine-independent C# with automated tests. All values are approximate and simplified for learning.

Code in this project was written with assistance from AI tools (Claude Code) and reviewed by the team.
